Encodings, errors and offsets

Source: vignettes/zuutf.Rmd
zuutf.Rmd
library(zuutf)

zuutf validates and converts text between UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32 and Latin-1 with the simdutf library, and says where the first error is. This vignette covers what it accepts, what it does with bad input, and how it counts positions.

Three shapes of input

Every function takes a character vector, a raw vector or a list of raw vectors. A raw vector is one element; a list holds one element per raw vector, and NULL is a missing one.

utf_valid(c("plain", "caf\u00e9", NA))
#> [1] TRUE TRUE   NA
utf_valid(as.raw(c(0x61, 0xff)))
#> [1] FALSE
utf_valid(list(charToRaw("ok"), as.raw(0xc0), NULL))
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE    NA

A character vector is text: each string is taken in its marked encoding and checked in its UTF-8 form. To check the bytes R holds instead, use useBytes = TRUE.

Encodings

The names are "UTF-8", "UTF-16LE", "UTF-16BE", "UTF-32LE", "UTF-32BE" and "Latin-1", matched without regard to case or hyphens. "ASCII" is for validation. On input, "UTF-16" and "UTF-32" let a byte-order mark choose, big-endian without one, and utf_decode() defaults to "auto", which asks utf_detect().

le <- utf_encode("na\u00efve", "UTF-16LE")
le
#>  [1] 6e 00 61 00 ef 00 76 00 65 00
utf_detect(le)
#> [1] "UTF-16LE" "UTF-16BE"
utf_decode(c(as.raw(c(0xff, 0xfe)), le))      # the BOM says little-endian
#> [1] "naïve"
utf_decode(le, "UTF-16LE")
#> [1] "naïve"

A leading byte-order mark that matches the input encoding is dropped, and no output carries one.

What happens to bad input

invalid chooses: an error, a replacement, or a missing value.

bad <- as.raw(c(0x61, 0xe2, 0x82, 0x62))      # "a", a cut-short euro sign, "b"
utf_decode(bad, "UTF-8", invalid = "replace")
#> [1] "a�b"
utf_decode(bad, "UTF-8", invalid = "na")
#> [1] NA
e <- tryCatch(utf_decode(bad, "UTF-8"), zuutf_encoding_error = function(e) e)
class(e)
#> [1] "zuutf_encoding_error" "zuutf_error"          "error"               
#> [4] "condition"
e$index
#> [1] 1
e$offset
#> [1] 2
e$encoding
#> [1] "UTF-8"

"replace" writes one U+FFFD for each maximal ill-formed subpart, as web browsers do, so the two bytes of the cut-short sequence above become one replacement character. In a Latin-1 target, which has no U+FFFD, it writes ?, and code points above U+00FF count as invalid too:

utf_encode("\u00e9t\u00e9 \u2600", "Latin-1", invalid = "replace")
#> [1] e9 74 e9 20 3f

R strings cannot hold U+0000, so decoding one to a string is an error under every policy. utf_convert() keeps it:

nul <- as.raw(c(0x61, 0x00, 0x62))
tryCatch(utf_decode(nul, "UTF-8"), zuutf_nul_error = function(e) e$offset)
#> [1] 2
utf_convert(nul, "UTF-8", "UTF-16LE")
#> [1] 61 00 00 00 62 00

Offsets

Offsets are 1-based, in the code units of the input: bytes for UTF-8 and Latin-1, 16-bit units for UTF-16, 32-bit units for UTF-32. They count from after any byte-order mark.

utf_error_at(as.raw(c(0x61, 0x62, 0xff)))
#> [1] 3
u16 <- c(as.raw(c(0xff, 0xfe)), utf_encode("ab", "UTF-16LE"), as.raw(c(0x00, 0xdc)))
utf_error_at(u16, "UTF-16")       # the lone surrogate is the third unit
#> [1] 3

Counting before converting

utf_count() counts code points, as nchar(type = "chars") does, and utf_length_as() says how many bytes a conversion will write:

x <- c("abc", "\u4e2d\u6587", "\U0001f600")
utf_count(x)
#> [1] 3 2 1
nchar(x)
#> [1] 3 2 1
utf_length_as(x, to = "UTF-16LE")
#> [1] 6 4 4

Base64

base64_encode() and base64_decode() work on one raw vector or one string. Decoding is forgiving by default, as browsers’ is; forgiving = FALSE reads RFC 4648 strictly.

s <- base64_encode(charToRaw("hello, world"))
s
#> [1] "aGVsbG8sIHdvcmxk"
rawToChar(base64_decode(s))
#> [1] "hello, world"
rawToChar(base64_decode(" aGVs\nbG8 "))
#> [1] "hello"
tryCatch(base64_decode("aGVsbG8", forgiving = FALSE),
         zuutf_base64_error = function(e) e$offset)
#> [1] 7

Which kernel ran

simdutf picks code for the processor at first use. zuutf_info() says which:

zuutf_info()$kernel
#> [1] "haswell"
